title: Montrose County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Montrose County wells have a 70-foot median depth and 10 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water-level records and checks before buying.
h1: What to Expect from a Well in Montrose County
intro_html:
A shallow well is common in Montrose County, but it is not a safe assumption for a land purchase. The recorded median depth is 70 feet, while the middle half spans 33-224 feet. That spread can change both the drilling bid and your site-development budget.

Colorado DWR records contain 3,926 permitted wells countywide, with 2,130 recorded as constructed. These are not all household supplies: monitoring accounts for 30% of the use mix. Start with the county figures, then narrow your comparison to nearby wells around Montrose, Olathe, Colona, Naturita, Nucla or Redvale.

sections.heading: A Shallow County Median, but a Wide Drilling Range
sections.html:
Of the 2,336 wells reporting depth, the median is 70 feet. The middle half runs from 33 to 224 feet, and 56% are under 100 feet. For a buyer, that means a shallow bid may be reasonable on some parcels, but the county median is not a depth guarantee.

Montrose County has mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. Permit aquifer labels are mostly unnamed or fractured bedrock, with Dakota and Dakota Sandstone also identified. Water-bearing layers and fractures can vary between sites. The 90th-percentile depth is 358 feet, so ask the driller to explain which neighboring completion records support the proposed depth and how additional footage will be charged.

sections.heading: What the Recorded Flow Means for a Household
sections.html:
The 413 reported pump yields have a median of 10 gpm, with the middle half between 5 and 15 gpm. That is an encouraging starting point for household planning, but a recorded pump yield does not establish how a well performs through sustained use or seasonal changes.

At the low end, 3% report under 1 gpm, and 17% fall in the 1-5 gpm category. A low-producing well can require storage and careful demand management. Before buying, request a current yield and recovery test rather than relying on an old permit entry. Also verify the permitted uses: a productive well does not automatically authorize irrigation or every planned use on the property.

sections.heading: Montrose County Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water, not the bottom of the well. Among 159 reported measurements, the county median is 32 feet below ground, and the middle half is 17-106 feet. Those measurements help describe pumping conditions, but they do not tell you how much water a well can deliver.

Decade medians were 22 feet in the 2000s, 45 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. This series does not show a steady drop in the water table. It also compares groups of measurements, not necessarily repeated readings from the same wells. For a particular property, seek dated measurements and pumping-test records from that well.

sections.heading: The County's Permit History and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
Montrose County's permit history stretches from 84 permits in the 1950s to a newest permit year of 2025. The largest listed decade was the 2000s, with 820 permits, followed by 495 in the 2010s and 361 in the 2020s. The latest decade is incomplete, and permit issuance is not the same as completed household-well construction.

Named drilling firms in the records include Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth), with 280 entries, and Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.), with 135. Historical entries are useful leads, not confirmation of current availability or licensing. Domestic/household uses account for 49% of the use mix, so compare records serving a similar purpose when evaluating a residential lot.

sections.heading: Budgeting for the Hole and the Finished Well
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $50-$75 per foot for drilling in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the county's 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,500-$5,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $9,500-$17,200.

Keep those scopes separate when comparing bids. A drilling price is not the price of water delivered to the house. Ask what the quote includes for casing, grout, testing, pump equipment and site access. Because the middle half of recorded depths reaches 224 feet, a median-depth allowance can be too lean for a deeper parcel. Get a site-specific estimate and written terms for additional drilling or an unsuccessful hole.

sections.heading: Environmental Flags, Low Yield and Septic Placement
sections.html:
The supplied environmental mapping identifies 28 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 7 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles. These are screening flags, not evidence that a particular private well is contaminated. Review the actual site locations and available findings, then choose water tests appropriate to the property.

Construction matters too: inspect the wellhead, surface drainage, casing and available grout records. Coordinate the well location with septic suitability, required setbacks, the house and driveway before fixing the building layout. Low yield deserves its own investigation. Missing construction or yield information does not prove a dry hole; obtain the completion report and test results rather than treating an incomplete permit record as a verdict.

sections.heading: Before Buying Land near Olathe, Nucla or Colona
sections.html:
Compare the parcel with nearby completed wells before leaning on the county average. Records around Olathe, Montrose or Colona should be checked locally, just as a parcel near Naturita, Nucla or Redvale needs its own neighboring-well review. Look for comparable ground, elevations, depths, reported yields and actual construction status.

For an existing home, match the well permit to the property and obtain the construction log, pump records, water-quality results and a current performance test. For vacant land, confirm DWR permit eligibility and allowed uses before committing to the build. Ask whether augmentation is required for the proposed use. Have the driller and site contractor coordinate access, well placement, septic and utility routing before finalizing the house location.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Montrose County?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth in Montrose County is 70 feet, based on 2,336 depth reports. The middle half ranges from 33 to 224 feet, and 56% are under 100 feet. Local sedimentary layers, alluvial deposits and bedrock conditions make nearby completion logs more useful for a parcel-specific estimate than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Montrose County?
faq.a: The local model estimates drilling at $50-$75 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, the hole costs about $3,500-$5,200, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $9,500-$17,200. Deeper drilling and site-specific construction needs can change the budget, so compare written bids with matching scopes.

faq.q: How much water do Montrose County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 10 gpm, with the middle half between 5 and 15 gpm. Only 413 wells report yield, so these figures are not a guarantee for every parcel. With 3% reporting under 1 gpm, buyers should obtain a current yield and recovery test and discuss storage if production is limited.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Montrose County?
faq.a: The county permit statistics cannot establish drinking-water safety. Environmental mapping lists 28 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 7 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles, but proximity does not prove contamination. Test the property's water, review nearby environmental findings and inspect the well's construction and condition before relying on it for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Montrose County?
faq.a: The supplied records do not show a steady decline. Median static water depths were 22 feet in the 2000s, 45 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. These are grouped measurements, not necessarily tracking the same wells. A property's dated water-level and pumping records are better evidence of its local trend.
